title: TikTok ad script template: stop staring at the blank page
markdown:
# TikTok ad script template: stop staring at the blank page

At 9:47 p.m., the footage is trimmed, the lighting looks good, and the edit is open on your phone. Then the cursor lands in the script box. Nothing. You know the point you want to make, but the first sentence has to earn the next 30 seconds, and suddenly every version sounds stiff.

If filming and editing are already your strengths, the problem is not that you need another course on TikTok. You need a usable first draft that gives the video a shape before you talk yourself out of posting it.

This TikTok ad script template is for that moment. Start with one clear subject, one audience, and the facts you can stand behind. The script should turn those into a claim, a few possible openings, and a filming plan you can revise. It should not pretend that every topic needs the same viral formula.

## Start with the point, not the hook

Hooks matter, but a hook has nowhere to go if the video has no point. Before writing, finish this sentence: "After watching, I want someone to believe or do ___."

That blank can be small. Maybe you want a freelancer to test cold outreach again. Maybe you want a skincare buyer to stop copying a routine that irritates their skin. A useful TikTok script makes one promise and pays it off. When a draft tries to squeeze in five tips, it usually becomes a list that nobody remembers.

Give yourself the raw material a writer would need:

- The claim you can support.
- The detail, example, result, or opinion that makes it worth hearing.
- The action you want the viewer to take after the video.

The useful constraint is honesty. If you did not get a 40% reply rate, do not borrow one for the hook. A strong script can use a sharp question or a surprising contrast without inventing proof.

## Build the 30 seconds around a change

Most short scripts need four jobs: stop the scroll, establish the tension, deliver the useful turn, and close with a next step. That is not a rigid timing rule. A tutorial may spend longer on the demonstration. A reaction video may reach the point faster. Still, the sequence prevents the common failure mode: a promising opening followed by thirty seconds of throat-clearing.

Try this rough outline:

1. Open with a claim or question that only makes sense if the viewer stays.
2. Name the familiar frustration or mistaken assumption.
3. Show the proof, method, or example that changes the picture.
4. End with one practical action, not a pile of requests to like, follow, comment, and buy.

The visual plan belongs beside the words. If the voiceover says "I changed one line," the screen should show the before and after, a close shot of the note, or you making the change. A script that only describes what the viewer could see is wasting the medium.

## Give yourself several openings

The first hook you write is often serviceable and forgettable. Ask for contrasting options instead: a contrarian claim, a question, and a fact-based opening. Choose the one that best matches what the video can actually prove.

This is especially useful when your instinct is to write a grand promise. "This will change your content" is vague and asks for trust. "I stopped opening my videos with the topic" gives a viewer something concrete to test. The best opening is not the loudest one. It is the one the rest of the video can carry.

## Make the draft easy to film

A script is only useful if it survives contact with a camera. Read it aloud once. Cut any sentence that you would not say to a friend. Replace broad claims with the visible detail that earns them. Then decide where the edit changes: a new shot, a screen recording, a text overlay, or a pause.

Keep the CTA proportionate. If the video teaches one small move, invite the viewer to try it or save the post. If you are selling something, say what it helps with and let the video do the persuasion. Pressure makes a short video feel longer.

## What the tool returns

Here is a real published example of the input and the shortened output:

**You send:** "A 30-second TikTok about why cold email still works in 2026."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Angle:** the single sharpest claim the video makes about cold email in 2026.
- **Hooks (3, one marked RECOMMENDED):**
  1. *Contrarian* — "Everyone says cold email is dead. It isn't." (RECOMMENDED, with the reason it works)
  2. *Question* — "Why did this cold email get a 40% reply rate?"
  3. *Stat-style* — a hook built only from facts you supplied.
- **Timed script table:** voiceover · on-screen text · visual/shot cue, beat by beat, HOOK → BUILD → PAYOFF → CTA.
- **Caption:** 4–6 hashtags plus one filming or posting tip.

If your bottleneck is the blank page, use [tiktok-script-pro](https://capafy.ai/agent/2844813315?ct=tiktok_blog) to get a structured draft, then make it sound like you before you record.
